report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **true**: high-quality evidence demonstrates that tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) started in the third trimester significantly reduces mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of hepatitis B virus (HBV) in pregnant women with high viral loads.

### Key Evidence
* **Landmark Clinical Trials:** A landmark randomized clinical trial published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* (Pan et al., 2016) showed that TDF initiated at 28–32 weeks of gestation in women with high HBV viral loads (HBV DNA ≥ 200,000 IU/mL) reduced transmission to infants from 18% down to 5% (per-protocol analysis) compared to standard care alone.
* **Global Guidelines:** Based on robust trial data and meta-analyses, the World Health Organization (WHO) and major professional societies (such as AASLD and EASL) formally recommend third-trimester TDF prophylaxis for pregnant women with high viral loads to prevent vertical transmission.

### Why Doubts Arise
Skepticism sometimes stems from trials conducted in settings where standard infant immunoprophylaxis (hepatitis B vaccine plus immunoglobulin within hours of birth) is so effective that baseline transmission rates are exceptionally low, occasionally yielding smaller absolute differences in intent-to-treat analyses. Nevertheless, clinical evidence consistently shows that infant immunoprophylaxis alone can fail in high-viral-load mothers, and TDF provides critical additional protection.

### Sources
* NEJM Clinical Trial: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1508660
* JAMA Trial Summary: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/article-abstract/2545684
* WHO Guidance on HBV MTCT: https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/hepatitis-preventing-mother-to-child-transmission-of-the-hepatitis-b-virus
* PMC Review on TDF Efficacy: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7488796/
